steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on learning inverse perception contracts for perception modules in autonomous systems. Motivate why perception error matters for safe control, connect it to earlier work on perception contracts, describe our approach and the quadcopter landing experiments, and list our contributions.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Perception in autonomous systems
- perception crucial for reacting and adapting in unstructured environments
- past decade: algorithms for obstacle detection/classification, pose estimation, localization

2. Perception error and safety
- real-world signals noisy; noise sometimes poorly understood and characterized
- perception output drives downstream decision/control -> errors can cause unwanted, even catastrophic actions
- reliable perception-based control for safety-critical systems: active research topic, recent attempts

3. Perception contracts and our inverse version
- approach: characterize perception error, then design controllers robust to it
- perception contracts (PC): characterize perception error, useful for proving system-level invariants
- PCs built automatically from data; used to verify vision-based lane-keeping systems
- our goal: controller synthesis instead
- inverse perception contracts (IPCs): perceived value -> perception error, i.e. uncertainty of the result
- downstream controller/decision modules compensate for uncertainty -> safety, robustness

4. Constructing an IPC
- perception estimates a quantity, e.g. obstacle position; ground truth y
- most algorithms give only a single-point estimate \hat{y}, a noisy version of y; robust control needs its uncertainty
- IPC: map \hat{y} -> set containing y with high probability, even under environmental variations
- neural network model; loss functions balance error vs conservativeness
- only needs data set of (\hat{y}, y) pairs; runs online, fast; uncertainty used for safe control signals

5. Quadcopter experiments and contributions
- quadcopter with camera; perception estimates landing pad pose from images
- learned IPC error below 0.2\% on testing set
- conservativeness: tuned perception parameters, IPC error under unseen parameters; output tight, adheres to training parameter
- robust control algorithm using IPC lands quadcopter safely despite significant perception error
- contributions: learn IPC from data automatically; IPC usable downstream to compensate upstream error; real-world evaluation

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Perception is crucial for modern autonomous systems to react and adapt in unstructured environments. In the past decade, perception algorithms have been invented for a variety of tasks, such as detection and classification of obstacles, pose estimation, and localization.

However, any interpretation of signals from the real world has to deal with noise, and this noise is sometimes poorly understood and characterized. The output of the perception module drives the downstream decision or control modules in an autonomous system, so errors in perception may lead to unwanted and even catastrophic actions. That is why designing reliable perception-based control algorithms for safety-critical systems has become an active research topic, and there are attempts in recent works.

One way to design reliable perception-based controllers is to first characterize the perception error and then design controllers that are robust to it. Recent works proposed the notion of perception contracts (PC) to address this problem. A PC characterizes the error of perception modules in a way that is useful for proving system-level invariants. The authors showed that perception contracts can be constructed automatically from data, and they used PCs to verify several vision-based lane-keeping systems. In this paper, we want to solve the controller synthesis problem instead. Inspired by the idea of PCs, we propose inverse perception contracts (IPCs), which map a perceived value to a perception error that characterizes the uncertainty of the perception result. The downstream controller and decision-making modules can then use the IPC to compensate for the uncertainty of the perception, and this helps make the autonomous system safer and more robust.

Constructing an IPC
- perception estimates a quantity, e.g. obstacle position; ground truth y
- most algorithms give only a single-point estimate \hat{y}, a noisy version of y; robust control needs its uncertainty
- IPC: map \hat{y} -> set containing y with high probability, even under environmental variations
- neural network model; loss functions balance error vs conservativeness
- only needs data set of (\hat{y}, y) pairs; runs online, fast; uncertainty used for safe control signals

Quadcopter experiments and contributions
- quadcopter with camera; perception estimates landing pad pose from images
- learned IPC error below 0.2\% on testing set
- conservativeness: tuned perception parameters, IPC error under unseen parameters; output tight, adheres to training parameter
- robust control algorithm using IPC lands quadcopter safely despite significant perception error
- contributions: learn IPC from data automatically; IPC usable downstream to compensate upstream error; real-world evaluation

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Perception is crucial for modern autonomous systems to react and adapt in unstructured environments. In the past decade, perception algorithms have been invented for a variety of tasks, such as detection and classification of obstacles, pose estimation, and localization.

However, any interpretation of signals from the real world has to deal with noise, and this noise is sometimes poorly understood and characterized. The output of the perception module drives the downstream decision or control modules in an autonomous system, so errors in perception may lead to unwanted and even catastrophic actions. That is why designing reliable perception-based control algorithms for safety-critical systems has become an active research topic, and there are attempts in recent works.

One way to design reliable perception-based controllers is to first characterize the perception error and then design controllers that are robust to it. Recent works proposed the notion of perception contracts (PC) to address this problem. A PC characterizes the error of perception modules in a way that is useful for proving system-level invariants. The authors showed that perception contracts can be constructed automatically from data, and they used PCs to verify several vision-based lane-keeping systems. In this paper, we want to solve the controller synthesis problem instead. Inspired by the idea of PCs, we propose inverse perception contracts (IPCs), which map a perceived value to a perception error that characterizes the uncertainty of the perception result. The downstream controller and decision-making modules can then use the IPC to compensate for the uncertainty of the perception, and this helps make the autonomous system safer and more robust.

In this paper, we look at perception modules that try to estimate the value of a specific quantity, for example, the position of an obstacle. Let y be the ground-truth value of this quantity. Most perception algorithms give only a single-point estimate \hat{y}, which can be seen as a noisy version of y. But to design robust controllers, we also need the uncertainty of the estimate \hat{y}. For this, we construct an IPC for the perception module, which is just a mapping from the perceived value \hat{y} to a set that contains the ground-truth value y with a high probability. This containment should hold even when the environment varies. We model the IPC with a neural network and carefully design loss functions so that they balance the error and the conservativeness of the IPC. The only thing needed to apply the approach is a data set of pairs of estimate \hat{y} and ground truth y. After it is trained on the data set, the IPC can run online and quickly compute the uncertainty of any estimate \hat{y}. Downstream modules can then use the computed uncertainty to compute safe control signals.

We evaluated the approach on a quadcopter that has a camera. The perception module we look at is a program that estimates the pose of a landing pad from camera images. Using the proposed approach, we constructed an accurate IPC for the perception module. Experimental results show that the error of the learned IPC was below 0.2\% on the testing set. To study how conservative the learned IPC is, we tuned some parameters of the perception module to change the characteristics of the perception error, and we measured and reported the error of the IPC under these unseen perception parameters. The results show that the output of the learned IPC is tight and adheres to the perception parameter it was trained under. Then, to show that the IPC can be used by downstream modules, we design a robust control algorithm that uses the learned IPC to safely land the quadcopter on the landing pad. Experiments show that with the learned IPC, the quadcopter can safely complete the landing task even though the perception error is significant.

Our contribution has three parts.

- We proposed an approach that learns an inverse perception contract from data automatically;

- We showed that downstream modules can use the learned inverse perception contract to compensate for the error of the upstream perception module;

- We evaluated the approach in a real-world application.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Perception is crucial for making modern autonomous systems react and adapt in unstructured environments. In the past decade, perception algorithms have been invented to perform a variety of tasks such as detection and classification of obstacles [1], pose estimation [2], and localization [3].

However, any interpretation of signals from the real world has to deal with noise, which is sometimes poorly understood and characterized. As the output of the perception module drives downstream decisions or control modules in an autonomous system, the errors in perception may result in unwanted and even catastrophic actions. Therefore, designing reliable perception-based control algorithms for safety-critical systems has become an active research topic, and attempts have been made in recent works, for example [4,5].

One way to design reliable perception-based controllers is to first characterize the perception error and then design controllers that are robust to the perception error. In a series of recent works [6,7], the notion of perception contracts (PC) has been proposed to address this problem. A PC characterizes the error of perception modules in a way that can be useful for proving system-level invariants. The authors have shown that such perception contracts can be constructed automatically from data and they used PCs to verify several vision-based lane-keeping systems [6,7]. In this paper, we want to solve the controller synthesis problem instead. Inspired by the idea of PCs, we proposed inverse perception contracts (IPCs) that map a perceived value to a perception error, which characterizes the uncertainty of the perception result. Such an IPC can then be used by the downstream controller and decision-making modules to compensate for the uncertainty of the perception, which helps enhance the safety and robustness of the autonomous system.

In this paper, we consider perception modules that aim to estimate the value of a specific quantity, for example, the position of an obstacle. Let y be the ground-truth value of this quantity. Most perception algorithms only provide a single-point estimate \hat{y}, which can be seen as a noisy version of y. However, in order to design robust controllers, the uncertainty of the estimate \hat{y} is also needed. For this, we construct an IPC for the perception module, which is simply a mapping from the perceived value \hat{y} to a set that contains the ground-truth value y with a high probability. This containment should hold even under environmental variations. We model the IPC using a neural network and carefully design loss functions that balance the error and conservativeness of the IPC. The only thing needed for applying the proposed approach is a data set that consists of pairs of estimate \hat{y} and ground truth y. Once trained on the data set, the IPC can be executed online and quickly compute the uncertainty of any estimate \hat{y}. The computed uncertainty can then be used by downstream modules to compute safe control signals.

We evaluated the proposed approach on a quadcopter that has a camera. The perception module of interest is a program that aims to estimate the pose of a landing pad from camera images. Using the proposed approach, we successfully constructed an accurate IPC for the perception module. Experimental results show that the error of the learned IPC was below 0.2\% on the testing set. In order to study the conservativeness of the learned IPC, we tuned some parameters of the perception module to change the characteristics of the perception error. We measured and reported the error of the IPC under these unseen perception parameters. Results show that the output of the learned IPC is tight and adheres to the perception parameter under which it was trained. Then, in order to show the IPC’s capability of being used by downstream modules, we design a robust control algorithm that utilizes the learned IPC and aims to safely land the quadcopter on the landing pad. Experiments show that with the learned IPC, the quadcopter can safely complete the landing task even though the perception error is significant.

In summary, our contribution has three parts.

- • We proposed an approach that can automatically learn an inverse perception contract from data;

- • We demonstrated that the learned inverse perception contract can be used by downstream modules to compensate for the error of the upstream perception module;

- • We evaluated the proposed approach in a real-world application.

References:

[2] Y. Xiang, T. Schmidt, V. Narayanan, and D. Fox, “Posecnn: A convolutional neural network for 6d object pose estimation in cluttered scenes,” arXiv preprint arXiv:1711.00199 , 2017.
[3] R. Mur-Artal, J. M. M. Montiel, and J. D. Tardos, “ORB-SLAM: a versatile and accurate monocular slam system,” IEEE transactions on robotics , vol. 31, no. 5, pp. 1147–1163, 2015.
[4] S. Dean, A. Taylor, R. Cosner, B. Recht, and A. Ames, “Guaranteeing safety of learned perception modules via measurement-robust control barrier functions,” in Conference on Robot Learning . PMLR, 2021, pp. 654–670.
[5] C. Dawson, B. Lowenkamp, D. Goff, and C. Fan, “Learning safe, generalizable perception-based hybrid control with certificates,” IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters , vol. 7, no. 2, pp. 1904–1911, 2022.
[6] C. Hsieh, Y. Li, D. Sun, K. Joshi, S. Misailovic, and S. Mitra, “Verifying controllers with vision-based perception using safe approximate abstractions,” IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems , vol. 41, no. 11, pp. 4205–4216, 2022.
